extracted.intended_audience: British political class and educated public interested in government and the French Revolution
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the legitimacy, prudence, and consequences of government policies and revolutionary measures, with emphasis on economic, legal, moral, and constitutional standards. The text lays out criteria for judging when reform is preferable to overthrow and what indicators show a government's fitness or failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable contribution/taxation among orders
rubrics_metrics.description: 'They ought to have paid annually about forty thousand pounds more, to put them on a par with the contribution of the nobility.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether privileged estates (clergy, nobility) contribute fairly to public burdens; compare actual payments and calculate required adjustments to parity. Used to judge whether grievances justify radical measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer negotiated contribution over confiscation
rubrics_metrics.description: The clergy made an offer of a contribution which 'for its extravagance, ought not to have been accepted' but would have been more advantageous than confiscation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider accepting voluntary or negotiated offers from institutions (e.g., Church) rather than resorting to confiscation; evaluate whether policy aims to make institutions serve the state or to destroy them as a political objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid flooding markets with mass sales of land
rubrics_metrics.description: 'To bring this unwieldy mass of landed property ... at once into market was obviously to defeat the profits proposed by the confiscation, by depreciating the value of those lands, and indeed of all the landed estates throughout France.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate fiscal/property reforms for their macroeconomic effect: mass disposals can depress asset values, harm landowners, and disrupt credit; plan sales to avoid market gluts and depreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetary prudence and respect for credit/property
rubrics_metrics.description: Compulsory paper currency and the creation of new paper founded on Church lands is described as 'so violent an outrage upon credit, property, and liberty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess monetary reforms for effects on credit, property rights, and liberty. Avoid issuing forced or depreciated currency that undermines confidence, confiscates value, or compels citizens to accept devalued instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve independent judicature
rubrics_metrics.description: 'To cut off all appearance of connection between the crown and public justice, ... the old independent judicature of the Parliaments, ... was wholly abolished.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge reforms by whether they maintain judicial independence; abolishing independent courts concentrates power and risks eliminating legal protections and ancient checks on arbitrary rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness of compensation to dispossessed officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Magistrates and officers 'had purchased their places ... Their compensation becomes part of the national debt' while clergy receive depreciated paper or starve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When removing officeholders, ensure compensation is fair and not paid in depreciated or morally tainted instruments; compensation mechanisms should not simply cloak expropriation or injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating a regime-dependent landed interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The text warns of creating 'a new landed interest connected with the new republic, and connected with it for its very being' and of binding the nation 'in one guilty interest to uphold this act.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether policies create classes whose economic survival depends on maintaining an unjust regime; such vested interests corrupt politics and coerce broader complicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit coercive enforcement of regime financial schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: They 'rendered their paper circulation compulsory in all payments.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat compulsory acceptance of government-issued instruments as an anti-pattern; financial instruments should be voluntary and credible, not enforced to coerce participation in political projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer mixed constitution and checks over pure extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: Burke advocates 'a monarchy directed by laws, controlled and balanced by the great hereditary wealth and hereditary dignity of a nation, and both again controlled by ... the reason and feeling of the people at large, acting by a suitable and permanent organ.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate constitutional arrangements by their capacity to balance elements (monarchy, aristocracy, popular representation) rather than adopting pure forms that risk degeneracy; prefer institutions that embed mutual checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against majority tyranny in democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: 'In a democracy the majority of the citizens is capable of exercising the most cruel oppressions upon the minority.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess democratic systems for protections of minorities and mechanisms preventing majoritarian abuse; consider historical tendencies toward factional persecution in unchecked democracies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population growth as indicator of government health
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The state of its population ... No country in which population flourishes ... can be under a _very_ mischievous government.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use demographic data—population size and growth trends—as one measure of whether government fosters prosperity and social stability; declining or stagnating population may signal misgovernance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wealth, distribution, and circulation as standards
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The wealth of a country is another, and no contemptible standard ... but I apprehend that her comparative wealth is much inferior to ours,--that it is not so equal in the distribution, nor so ready in the circulation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate economy by total wealth, equality of distribution, and fluidity of circulation; a government that hinders circulation or creates unequal distribution may be judged defective even with large population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic culture, arts, and infrastructure as measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Burke lists roads, bridges, ports, harbors, manufactures, arts, science, fortifications as evidence that the French monarchy was not wholly oppressive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider investment in public works, arts, sciences, and manufacturing as evidence of a government's constructive effects; these are signs that institutions sustained civilization despite abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer reformation over total demolition when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The question ... is, whether those who would have reformed or those who have destroyed are in the right.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether identified abuses could be corrected by reform within existing structures rather than by wholesale overthrow; weigh the costs of destruction against the possibilities of gradual improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity and proportionality of revolutionary measures
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Men have been sometimes led by degrees, sometimes hurried, into things of which, if they could have seen the whole together, they never would have permitted the most remote approach.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate revolutions by whether actors had full knowledge and whether measures were proportionate; beware of accumulative steps leading to disproportionate outcomes that contemporaries might not have sanctioned knowingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical assessment before punitive measures against classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Burke argues nobility and clergy were painted as objects of horror but asks whether they deserved exile, torture, confiscation, or abolition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before punitive collective measures (exile, property seizure, abolition of orders), require concrete evidence of systematic oppression; avoid collective punishment based on caricature or rhetorical vilification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess actual behavior of elites toward lower classes
rubrics_metrics.description: 'As to their behavior to the inferior classes, they appeared to me to comport themselves towards them with good-nature ... To strike any person ... was a thing in a manner unknown.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use eyewitness and documentary evidence of landlords' conduct—treatment of tenants, fairness of rents, abuses—to judge legitimacy of targeting elites; avoid broad-brush condemnations contrary to observed conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider municipal distress and inclusion in reforms
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The municipalities had been ... reduced to the most deplorable indigence. Money was nowhere to be seen. They ... panted for a currency ...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for local governments' fiscal condition and include them in equitable solutions; exclusion or sudden appropriation of local assets can produce unrest and practical failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor specie and currency availability as health metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: M. Necker's estimates of specie contrasted with 'present disappearance of coin' and employment decline in Paris.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track hard currency (specie) levels, money supply, and employment as early warning indicators of economic collapse; reconciliations between official claims and market reality are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh long-term recovery costs in revolutionary change
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Instead of improving by the change, I apprehend that a long series of years must be told, before it can recover in any degree the effects of this philosophic Revolution.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor in multi-year costs, population loss, emigration, decline in commerce and employment when judging the prudence of radical change; short-term zeal may obscure long-term harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral-legal legitimacy of measures affecting property and liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: The text repeatedly condemns 'frauds, impostures, violences, rapines, burnings, murders, confiscations, compulsory paper currencies' as abuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate policies against standards of legality, property rights, and moral restraint; measures that rely on violence, expropriation, or deceit lack legitimacy even if politically expedient.
